questions.question: How do Jest and Vitest work — describe the testing patterns: mocks, async, table-driven tests, and setup.
questions.title: Vitest Jest Basics
questions.direct_answer: Jest (and its Vite-native sibling Vitest) provide: test() blocks with describe() grouping; expect() matchers (toBe — identity, toEqual — deep, toContain, toHaveBeenCalledWith); beforeEach/afterEach for per-test setup/teardown; jest.mock/fn for test doubles; and native async handling (return the promise or await it — the test waits). Table-driven: array of [input, expected], forEach → test per row — one test body, many cases, failures name the row.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    F[test file → own worker: isolated module state] --> D[describe: grouped hooks]
    D --> T[test blocks: sequential] 
    T --> A[assert via expect matchers]
    M[mocks: spy / stub / fn / fake] --> B[boundary only: network, time, 3rd-party]
    TBL[table-driven: rows → one body] --> ROW[failure names the row]
    ASYNC[await or return the promise] --> W[runner waits, catches rejection]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The parallelism/isolation model (how the runner works): each test FILE runs in its own worker/module context — module state doesn't leak between files, which is why tests within a file share top-level setup but files are independent. Within a file, tests run sequentially by design; describe blocks group for shared beforeEach hooks. The flakiness rule: a test that depends on execution order or shared mutable state passes in isolation and fails in the suite — the debugging discipline is run-single-file first, then the suite.

The mock taxonomy (the precision that shows expertise): spies (wrap the real function, record calls — jest.spyOn for verifying 'did we call console.error' without changing behavior), stubs (replace with canned returns — the fetch mock returning a fixture), mocks proper (recording fakes with programmable behavior — jest.fn().mockResolvedValue(x)), and fakes (working lightweight implementations — an in-memory db). The rule: use the LEAST powerful double that answers the question — a spy when you need to verify a call, a stub when you need to control a return, never a mock where a real pure function would do.

The async edge cases (the bug classes worth naming): floating promises — an async test that doesn't await asserts nothing but passes (enable no-floating-promises or return the promise); timer tests — debounce/interval logic needs jest.useFakeTimers + advanceTimersByTime (real timers make tests slow and flaky); and unhandled rejections between tests poison the NEXT test — afterEach cleanup isn't optional for anything subscription-based. The professional close: test pyramid proportions (many pure-logic units, fewer component tests, few E2E) exist because each layer up costs ~10x more runtime — and the slow layers exist to catch what the fast ones structurally can't.
